W&B audit: GRPO reward variation and late EvalPlus plateau
Run: `kunal-personal/grpo-mbpp/mbpphard10x1009`, display name `grpo-mbpp-fulltrain-8x16-b128-micro2-workers8-0.5b-50000-dual-greedy-evalplus031-visible1-save10-10x-harder-luna-20261009`. The run ended in crashed state with last heartbeat 2026-10-11 06:33:45 UTC. Config: `configs/grpo-mbpp-fulltrain-8x16-b128-micro2-workers8-0.5b-50000-dual-greedy-evalplus031-visible1-save10-10x-harder-luna-20261009.yaml`; 5,910 original plus hard-synthetic tasks, 16 generations per task, DAPO loss, learning rate 1e-5, beta 0.01, hybrid reward coefficient 0.75, one visible assertion in the prompt, and reward scoring over all saved assertions. Code baseline before this record: commit `edb1099f8b5435e563f71d782d3b8a859b6164e4`.

Reward history audit: W&B returned 191 sampled rows with the rollout diagnostics across the run, so these aggregates are descriptive samples rather than an exhaustive recomputation. Mean individual-assertion pass fraction was 30.6%; by chronological thirds of the returned points it rose from 23.8% to 29.8% to 38.0%. Mean full-candidate pass fraction rose from 7.1% to 8.3% to 16.7%. Mean within-task group reward standard deviation was 0.121 overall and rose from 0.105 in the first third to 0.151 in the last third. The fraction of flat groups, where all 16 candidates had the same reward, averaged 17.3%. Thus most sampled prompt groups had reward variation, and that variation did not disappear as the run progressed. The assertion-pass fraction is a candidate-level assertion ratio, not task pass@1. `reward/full_pass_fraction` is the fraction of sampled candidates passing every stored assertion.

Evaluation history: The W&B read returned 134 recorded EvalPlus points from evaluation step 0 through 1,330. MBPP pass@1 started at 52.4%, peaked at 63.2% at step 1,250, and ended at 60.6%. MBPP+ pass@1 started at 43.7%, peaked at 54.0% at step 940, and ended at 51.9%. From step 900 to 1,330, training greedy pass@1 rose from 18.5% to 20.6%, while MBPP fell from 61.9% to 60.6% and MBPP+ fell from 52.9% to 51.9%. This supports late train/evaluation divergence despite increasing sampled reward and reward variation.

Interpretation: The audit does not support zero-variation groups as the main cause of the late plateau, so dynamic resampling of flat groups is not the first recommended change. The existing hybrid reward already gives 75% weight to complete test-suite success and 25% to assertion fraction. More training tests may improve reward quality, but the current history alone does not show that sparse or weak tests caused the plateau. A higher-value next comparison is continuing the same GRPO recipe from the best saved checkpoint with a lower learning rate against an unchanged continuation, evaluating both on the same full EvalPlus protocol and keeping the best checkpoint by held-out score. The step-940 checkpoint is best on MBPP+ in this run; step 1,250 is best on MBPP base. The goal metric must determine which checkpoint is the starting point.

Limitations: Reward rows were sampled by W&B history retrieval and split into approximate chronological thirds. No candidate replay, reward recomputation, new model generation, or test-set modification was performed. The 50-task pass@16 comparison is a separate sampled evaluation and is not directly interchangeable with full-set greedy EvalPlus.

GRPO plateau hypothesis audit with source and task transitions
Purpose: Identify the strongest observed bottleneck in GRPO run `mbpphard10x1009` and test the follow-up questions about reward coverage, source-specific learning, and gains versus regressions.
Run: `kunal-personal/grpo-mbpp/mbpphard10x1009`, display name `grpo-mbpp-fulltrain-8x16-b128-micro2-workers8-0.5b-50000-dual-greedy-evalplus031-visible1-save10-10x-harder-luna-20261009`. W&B URL: https://wandb.ai/kunal-personal/grpo-mbpp/runs/mbpphard10x1009. The run ended in crashed state at optimizer evaluation step 1,330. No process was started or stopped for this audit.
Setup: Base model `Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct`; LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05; DAPO objective; learning rate 1e-5; beta 0.01; BF16; 16 completions per prompt group; hybrid reward with coefficient 0.75 on full test-suite success and 0.25 on assertion fraction; maximum completion length 2,048; three-second sandbox timeout. Training used 591 original MBPP tasks and 5,319 harder synthetic tasks, for 5,910 tasks total. Synthetic artifact: `analysis/mbpp_category_synthetic_tasks_harder5319.jsonl`, SHA256 `7e120dd9b7891f3b5a057cfb438734345a73ed2b93b01d9e8239577e74350098`. Source config is `configs/grpo-mbpp-fulltrain-8x16-b128-micro2-workers8-0.5b-50000-dual-greedy-evalplus031-visible1-save10-10x-harder-luna-20261009.yaml`. The run's 591 original tasks are disjoint from the 378 canonical EvalPlus task IDs. The loader also removes normalized matching prompt text. Candidate training rewards use the configured training assertions. EvalPlus is a held-out measurement, not a training signal.
Evidence sources and limits: W&B history returned 500 sampled rollout rows per selected reward key over `_step` 198 to 268,473. The 134 greedy training-evaluation rows from step 0 to 1,330 were all returned. Local task-level training outputs cover all 5,910 tasks at each listed checkpoint. Local EvalPlus outputs cover all 378 tasks at steps 900, 1,250, and 1,330. W&B rollout samples are not a full replay and do not include source-stratified rollout rewards.
Reward and optimization findings: Sampled rollout `reward/flat_group_fraction` averaged 17.3%, 16.6%, and 19.2% across the first, second, and third chronological thirds. Thus about 81% to 83% of sampled task groups had reward variation. Mean group reward standard deviation rose from 0.103 to 0.137 to 0.139. Sampled candidate assertion pass fraction rose from 26.1% to 34.8% to 38.1%; sampled full-candidate pass fraction rose from 7.0% to 12.8% to 16.1%. The full-pass rate remained much lower than partial assertion success, so sparse complete solutions and partial-reward credit assignment remain plausible contributors. They did not worsen across training.
W&B optimizer history showed mean KL rising from 0.0184 to 0.0327 to 0.0426 across sampled thirds, while mean learning rate changed only from 9.95e-6 to 9.87e-6 to 9.78e-6. Mean entropy declined from 0.279 to 0.228 to 0.220. Mean gradient norm remained moderate and increased from 0.105 to 0.121 to 0.132. These observations support policy drift under a nearly constant learning rate as a candidate late-stage bottleneck. They do not show a numerical instability or prove that the learning rate caused the EvalPlus decline.
Source-specific greedy training results: At step 0, 197/591 originals passed all tests (33.33%) and 302/5,319 hard synthetic tasks passed (5.68%). At step 900, results were 247/591 (41.79%) and 847/5,319 (15.92%). At step 1,250, results were 263/591 (44.50%) and 973/5,319 (18.29%). At step 1,330, results were 265/591 (44.84%) and 950/5,319 (17.86%). Both sources improved substantially from baseline. From step 900 to 1,250, exact task transitions showed 34 original gains and 18 losses, and 233 synthetic gains and 107 losses. From step 1,250 to 1,330, originals had 22 gains and 20 losses, while synthetic tasks had 114 gains and 137 losses. The late synthetic regression is real in these saved greedy outputs, but its magnitude is small relative to the full pool. The data do not support synthetic-task interference as the sole or clearly dominant cause.
Overall training results: Greedy pass@1 increased from 8.44% at step 0 to 18.51% at step 900 and 20.91% at step 1,250, then eased to 20.56% at step 1,330. Test-pass fraction changed from 27.43% at step 0 to 41.34%, 43.79%, and 43.58% at those same checkpoints. Average reward changed from 0.272 to 0.411, 0.432, and 0.431. This indicates a broad learning plateau at the end rather than continued progress hidden by the training metric.
Held-out transitions: Full EvalPlus MBPP pass@1 was 63.2% at step 1,250 and 60.6% at step 1,330. MBPP+ was 53.2% and 51.9%. Compared with step 900, step 1,250 gained 14 MBPP tasks and lost 9; MBPP+ gained 8 and lost 8. From step 1,250 to 1,330, MBPP gained 1 and lost 11, while MBPP+ gained 3 and lost 7. The held-out decline is concentrated in a small number of discordant tasks. The checkpoint peak was selected after examining these same benchmark results, so it is a descriptive best observed point and not an unbiased final test estimate. The run still ended 8.2 percentage points above its initial MBPP and MBPP+ scores of 52.4% and 43.7%.
Interpretation: The strongest supported bottleneck is late optimization and generalization saturation under continuing policy drift. Reward diversity did not vanish, training metrics rose for most of the run, and both data sources improved. Yet in the final interval the training pass rate stopped improving, the synthetic portion regressed, and held-out pass rates fell. A high nearly constant learning rate and rising KL are plausible contributors. The full-candidate reward gap is a secondary concern because most rollouts still provided partial feedback and the sampled full-pass fraction rose over time. The size and quality of the hard synthetic mixture are plausible secondary risks, but this run alone cannot isolate their causal effect. There is no pass@16 measurement on EvalPlus in this audit, so it cannot determine whether sampling already reaches the intended pass@1 ceiling.
Next discriminating experiment: Compare two continuations from the same saved checkpoint and seed, one at the existing learning rate and one at a lower learning rate. Keep the data, generation count, reward, optimizer, and evaluation protocol fixed. Evaluate the full 378-task EvalPlus set at matched optimizer intervals and report both MBPP and MBPP+. Include the fixed training-set greedy metrics and KL so a held-out change can be compared with policy drift. A source-balanced or original-only control can follow if lower learning rate does not improve generalization. If ranking checkpoints by EvalPlus, treat that benchmark as development data and reserve an independent evaluation before claiming final generalization.
Artifacts: Config above; synthetic data SHA256 above; all per-task training predictions in `outputs/grpo-mbpp-fulltrain-8x16-b128-micro2-workers8-0.5b-50000-dual-greedy-evalplus031-visible1-save10-10x-harder-luna-20261009/training-step-{0,900,1250,1330}-details.json`; summary metrics beside those files; EvalPlus predictions in the same run directory at `evalplus/step-{900,1250,1330}/mbpp/qwen2_chat_temp_0.0/eval_results.json`; checkpoints include `checkpoint-940` and `checkpoint-1250`. The step-1,250 evaluation record lists code commit `32cd7cb`; the final evaluation record lists `49103a5`. Retrieval code and environment: W&B sampled history API; local JSON aggregation with Python 3; config enables BF16, per-task stop masking, fixed one-completion greedy evaluation, and no benchmark-based automatic checkpoint selection. No code, model, tests, checkpoints, or training processes were changed.

Router overfit experiment: MiniLM on one balanced MBPP batch
Purpose: Confirm that the small text encoder and binary classification head can fit a single batch of task-level cheap-model success labels.

The next controlled run should split original training tasks into a stratified train and validation set, use validation PR-AUC or F1 for checkpoint selection and early stopping, and reserve EvalPlus for one final benchmark. Given the small labeled dataset, first try a frozen encoder with a regularized head or unfreeze only the final encoder layers, with a lower learning rate. Tune the positive-class threshold on validation data because the fixed argmax threshold caused large precision and recall swings.


OPENCODEINSTRUCT ONLINE ROUTER EXPERIMENT
Status: Implementation committed before launch.
Purpose: Increase router training diversity by sampling OpenCodeInstruct tasks and generating Qwen 0.5B success labels in streaming batches.
Dataset: `nvidia/OpenCodeInstruct`, pinned revision `8f3ba5bafe4d6e8db46082cf7ae6741bc370604d`, dataset card license CC-BY-4.0. Source fields used are `id`, `input`, `output`, `unit_tests`, `domain`, and `generation_algorithm`. Source `tests_execution_status` and `average_test_score` are not used as labels.
Selection: Seed 42, Hugging Face streaming shuffle buffer 10,000, up to 20,000 selected source rows. Selection is based on stream order and exact prompt deduplication before labels are calculated. Exact prompt overlap with held-out EvalPlus task text is excluded. After selection, the supplied reference solution is run against the complete test suite to reject broken or unsafe test suites. This is a test-quality check; it does not determine the Qwen label.
Labeling: Exactly one temperature-zero Qwen 0.5B completion per valid task, top-p 1, max 2,048 tokens. Process source rows in batches of 8. Label 1 only when the completion passes the full validated test suite; otherwise label 0. Persist each completion and label in a SQLite cache keyed by dataset revision, task ID and content, checkpoint fingerprint, prompt version, and decoding policy. Commit after every batch.
Safety: Parse test arrays as JSON. Run supplied and generated Python only after static import and builtin checks, in a subprocess with filesystem and network audit blocks, process and memory limits, output-file limits, and a 5-second timeout.
Classifier: `microsoft/MiniLM-L12-H384-uncased`, trainable encoder, dropout 0.1, linear two-class CLS head, AdamW learning rate 5e-5, batch size 16, one epoch, max input length 512. Log loss each optimizer step. Evaluate full labeled training data and the existing 378-task EvalPlus set at baseline and every 100 optimizer steps. Report accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 for training, EvalPlus MBPP, and EvalPlus MBPP+ separately. Save step-100 and final models.
Artifacts: `outputs/router-opencode-online-20261013/`, including task labels, rejected test-suite records, persistent SQLite cache, metrics, predictions, and checkpoints. W&B project `kunal-personal/grpo-mbpp`; run name `router-opencode-online-minilm-20261013`.
Pilot diagnostics: In the first 100 unshuffled dataset rows, 49 supplied answers passed all tests, 45 failed, 4 had syntax errors, and 2 timed out. In a 1,000-row seed-42 shuffled sample, domain counts were generic 604 and algorithmic 396; generation methods were self-instruct 791 and evol-instruct 209. These diagnostics informed validation and are not training metrics.
Results: Pending. The training run and its W&B URL, final retrieval metrics, row counts, cache counts, duration, environment, and commit identifier will be appended after completion.

This is an early nine-batch snapshot, not an estimate of the eventual training distribution. Partial rewards allow variation even when all16 candidates fail full correctness.

Observed progression: Mixed-task-group fraction falls from0.8025 to0.41 and mean within-task reward standard deviation from0.2369 to0.1034. Training pass@1 rises from0.605396 at step700 to0.703204 at step1300, while MBPP changes from0.637566 to0.632275. This supports reduced task-level signal as a plausible contributor to slowdown, but training continues to improve and41percent of final-interval groups remain varied. The benchmark plateau therefore cannot be attributed to complete loss of training signal. Limited transfer to unseen tasks can coexist with declining diversity.

Limitations:13 serially dependent intervals from one run, with12 rollout mean changes. Raw correlations share a strong training-time trend; after linear step adjustment their signs reverse. This does not identify a causal effect of diversity. Lower nonzero reward standard deviation is not automatically weaker normalized GRPO advantage. Stochastic rollout means also change with sampled tasks. The original endpoint and initialization benchmarks are fixed historical measurements. Independent agent verification confirms all1300-step coverage,800 groups per interval, metric counts and key correlations.

Diagnosis: Training class prevalence is195/591=0.329949. Unweighted cross entropy on fixed features can favor scores near the majority-negative prior when the features separate labels weakly. At0.5 the training classifier returns all negatives and has zero positive recall/F1. The latest evaluation classifier has a small number of positive predictions, so its F1 is low rather than zero. The first zero training F1 occurred atstep200. Training AUPRC above prevalence and ROC-AUC above0.5 show some ranking discrimination; neither establishes useful selective routing at high precision. Lower threshold F1 can be close to a trivial all-positive baseline. This is consistent with limited linear separability of the frozen CLS representation, not demonstrated full-encoder overfitting. No numerical NaN or training crash is observed in the latest losses.

Definitions: ROC-AUC integrates true-positive rate against false-positive rate across score thresholds and has random-ranking baseline0.5. AUPRC is reported here as average precision, the step-integral of precision against recall with equal scores grouped. Its no-skill baseline is positive prevalence: train0.329949, MBPP0.515873, MBPP+0.447090. F1 is evaluated at a particular threshold, so nonzero ranking areas can coexist with zero F1 at0.5.

ROUTER CAPACITY COMPARISON: FROZEN HEAD VS LAST MINILM BLOCK, 2026-10-14

Purpose. Test whether the frozen MiniLM CLS representation underfits the original MBPP router labels, and whether training the final MiniLM transformer block plus the binary head improves validation ranking. Compare both modes on the same task split. Select checkpoints using only a validation split from original training tasks. Use EvalPlus only for one final measurement after selection.

Data. Training source is outputs/router-mbpp-original-one-shot-20261013/router_dataset.jsonl, SHA-256 3f53ff270d4a6b1900baa308e17a9d9d8e7e328f0717bee23d2da2f21a8115f9. It has591 original task labels from one greedy 0.5B completion per task, with195 positive and396 negative MBPP labels. The fixed seed42, 80/20 stratified split groups normalized task text. It yields473 training tasks with156 positives and317 negatives, plus118 validation tasks with39 positives and79 negatives. There is no normalized task-text overlap. Three duplicate-text pairs remain in one fold each. The EvalPlus source is outputs/router-evalplus-greedy-dual-label-20261013/router_evalplus_labels.jsonl, SHA-256 39b40772576bcdcdf858c71f9b1774d9dca1e30215d6eb99c85c89d2a0ab6531. It has378 tasks, with195 MBPP positives and169 MBPP+ positives. The labels were generated independently of this classifier training.

Model and setup. microsoft/MiniLM-L12-H384-uncased at revision44acabbec0ef496f6dbc93adadea57f376b7c0ec, CLS pooling, dropout0.1, and Linear(384,2). Loss is unweighted cross entropy. Both modes use seed42, batch16, input length512, AdamW, head learning rate5e-5, 30 epochs,900 optimizer updates, validation each30 updates, and no early stopping. The frozen baseline trains only the770-parameter head. The candidate trains the final MiniLM block with learning rate5e-6 plus the head, for1,775,234 trainable parameters. Each run selects the checkpoint with highest validation average precision. A trained checkpoint must beat the step-zero pretrained-MiniLM/random-head checkpoint. Each selected checkpoint receives one final EvalPlus evaluation. Both complete runs used an NVIDIA RTX A5000, Python3.12.3, PyTorch2.8.0+cu128, and Transformers4.56.2. Training code commit is74c4ace.

Runs. Frozen baseline W&B run 8pkm8x3a: https://wandb.ai/kunal-personal/grpo-mbpp/runs/8pkm8x3a, artifacts and history under outputs/router-minilm-original-frozen-30epochs-20261014. Last-block candidate W&B run ehjbs150: https://wandb.ai/kunal-personal/grpo-mbpp/runs/ehjbs150, artifacts and history under outputs/router-minilm-last-layer-30epochs-20261014. Both W&B runs log per-update loss, training and validation accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUPRC, trapezoidal PR area, ROC-AUC, prevalence, and threshold metrics from0.1 through0.9. Local histories include predictions and full metrics. The short five-check early-stopped pilot runs wwfanpro and xjzr2tdr are superseded by these full-budget runs.

Results at optimizer step900, before restoring the selected checkpoint. Frozen head: training loss0.6341, AUPRC0.3615, ROC-AUC0.5078; validation loss0.6351, AUPRC0.3056, ROC-AUC0.4580. Last block plus head: training loss0.6329, AUPRC0.3937, ROC-AUC0.5838; validation loss0.6357, AUPRC0.3077, ROC-AUC0.4466. Validation positive prevalence is0.3305. For both runs, the highest validation AUPRC is the initial step-zero value0.3575. No trained checkpoint improves it, so both select step0. The candidate improves training ranking but validation AUPRC remains below prevalence and ROC-AUC falls below0.5. The top block therefore increases training fit without improving this validation result.

Final EvalPlus metrics on each selected step-zero checkpoint are identical. MBPP AUPRC0.5808, ROC-AUC0.5645, F1 0.6806. MBPP+ AUPRC0.5252, ROC-AUC0.5675, F1 0.6179. At threshold0.5 the selected model predicts every task positive. Its F1 equals the all-positive baseline for each benchmark. Threshold sweeps are recorded in W&B and evaluation_history.jsonl; no benchmark threshold is selected.

Interpretation and limits. The last-block model does not reproduce near-perfect training memorization seen in prior full-encoder runs, but its train-validation ranking gap is consistent with overfitting on this small split. Both models' cross-entropy losses fall sharply as predictions move toward the class prior, while ranking quality does not improve. Loss reduction alone is therefore not evidence that the router learned useful task discrimination. This is one fixed split with39 validation positives and one-completion labels, so metric uncertainty is high. The identical final EvalPlus result is expected because checkpoint selection chose step0. These metrics do not show that the trained last-layer model improves generalization.

ROUTER REPRODUCTION: LAST THREE MINILM BLOCKS, 1,000 STEPS, 2026-10-14

Purpose. Reproduce the original-only overfit router experiment while limiting training to the final three MiniLM transformer blocks and the binary head. This isolates the effect of reducing trainable capacity. The requested budget was1,000 optimizer steps.

Data and labels. Training used all591 original MBPP training task labels from outputs/router-mbpp-original-one-shot-20261013/router_dataset.jsonl. Labels came from one greedy Qwen0.5B completion per task. The file SHA-256 is3f53ff270d4a6b1900baa308e17a9d9d8e7e328f0717bee23d2da2f21a8115f9. Evaluation used378 EvalPlus task rows from outputs/router-evalplus-greedy-dual-label-20261013/router_evalplus_labels.jsonl. This file contains separate MBPP and MBPP+ labels and has SHA-25639b40772576bcdcdf858c71f9b1774d9dca1e30215d6eb99c85c89d2a0ab6531. Training and evaluation IDs are separate. Each label is based on one model completion.

Model and training setup. The encoder is microsoft/MiniLM-L12-H384-uncased at pinned revision44acabbec0ef496f6dbc93adadea57f376b7c0ec, with CLS pooling. The classifier head is Dropout(0.1) followed by Linear(384,2), with770 parameters. The final three of twelve transformer blocks are trainable. The embedding layer, first nine blocks and pooler are frozen. Trainable encoder parameters total5,323,392, for5,324,162 parameters overall. The baseline run acamdajj trained all33,360,000 encoder parameters plus770 head parameters.

The run used seed42, batch size16, evaluation batch size32, maximum sequence length512, AdamW with default weight decay, cross entropy, and learning rate5e-5 for the head and unfrozen blocks. DYNAMIC FEW-SHOT RETRIEVAL FOR MBPP, 2026-10-15

Purpose. Measure greedy MBPP and MBPP+ pass@1 when each evaluation task receives its top-k nearest original MBPP training examples, for k=1, 2, 3, 4, and 8. Compare the results with the requested historical no-retrieval reference. No new k=0 evaluation is included.

Data and embeddings. The retrieval pool contains 591 original MBPP training tasks only. It excludes OpenCode tasks. The evaluation pool contains 378 EvalPlus MBPP tasks. Each task description was embedded once with OpenAI text-embedding-3-large at 3,072 dimensions. The saved embedding artifact is outputs/dynamic-few-shot-original-mbpp-20261014/embeddings.npz. Its input total was 16,560 tokens: 591 training tasks and 378 evaluation tasks. Training task data SHA-256 is d969fda2822cad2f83726f58d4a1a7adb228fd0ee43fc7c2702834313bab506e. Embeddings SHA-256 is 5df46ae7d52840e1a504568da950e0b4de684f7a7e74ba364a59342c12e6ed06.

Method and configuration. For each evaluation task, cosine similarity ranks the 591 training task description embeddings. The top k original tasks are added to the prompt with their descriptions, assertions, and reference code. Retrieval does not use evaluation labels or ground-truth solutions. Candidate selection is therefore independent of benchmark ground truth. Ground truth was used only by the separate EvalPlus scoring step. The generated answer came from Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct with the original MBPP-only GRPO adapter at checkpoint 830. Decoding was greedy with temperature 0, top_p 1, and at most 2,048 new tokens. EvalPlus scored all 378 tasks on base MBPP and MBPP+ tests. The evaluation ran on CPU with one Torch thread and low process priority while the separate GRPO job continued on GPU.

Results. The historical reference is the user's requested 52.9% MBPP pass@1 at step 40, paired with 43.9% MBPP+ pass@1 from the existing step-40 EvalPlus record. This is a prior checkpoint measurement, not a newly run k=0 condition, and it is not a controlled same-checkpoint comparison with checkpoint 830.

JEV TEN-CALL VOTE AGGREGATION FOR EVALPLUS MBPP, 2026-10-15

Purpose. Measure Jev as a yes/no router for whether one greedy Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct completion can pass all tests. Make ten independent Jev calls per task and compare single-call accuracy with three vote rules on the same 378 EvalPlus MBPP tasks.

Data and selection. Jev received each task prompt only. It did not receive Qwen completions or benchmark labels. Ten calls were made for every one of the 378 prompts, for 3,780 decisions total. After all calls were complete, each probability was converted to a vote at threshold 0.5. The MBPP and MBPP+ labels were then joined separately to measure accuracy. No task or vote rule was selected using labels. The EvalPlus prompt and label data is outputs/router-evalplus-greedy-dual-label-20261013/router_evalplus_labels.jsonl, SHA-256 39b40772576bcdcdf858c71f9b1774d9dca1e30215d6eb99c85c89d2a0ab6531.

Model and calls. The Typesafe System One API endpoint was https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Requested alias was jev-latest, and all 3,780 responses identified jev-1.13.0. Each call asked whether one first-try greedy Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct completion for the task could pass every task test. The same task prompt and question were sent ten times; the API does not expose seed control. Calls ran with 48 concurrent workers and used the existing repository .env JEV_API_KEY. Total reported usage was 1,524,310 input tokens and 83,160 output tokens.

Decision rules. A single-call vote predicts yes when that call's probability is at least 0.5. The single-call summary below is the mean accuracy across the ten call positions; the individual accuracies are also listed. Strict majority predicts yes only when at least six of ten votes are yes, so a 5-5 tie is no. Any-yes predicts yes if at least one vote is yes. The no-if-any-no rule predicts yes only when all ten calls vote yes.

Accuracy results:

| Vote rule | EvalPlus MBPP | EvalPlus MBPP+ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Single call, mean across 10 calls | 60.4% (228.5/378 mean) | 54.7% (206.7/378 mean) |
| Strict majority yes | 60.6% (229/378) | 54.8% (207/378) |
| Yes if any call says yes | 59.0% (223/378) | 53.2% (201/378) |
| Yes only if all calls say yes | 62.2% (235/378) | 56.9% (215/378) |

The ten single-call accuracies by call index were MBPP: 59.5%, 60.8%, 59.8%, 60.3%, 60.8%, 61.1%, 60.1%, 61.1%, 59.8%, and 61.1%. MBPP+ was 53.7%, 55.0%, 54.0%, 54.5%, 55.0%, 55.3%, 54.2%, 55.8%, 54.0%, and 55.3%. The standard deviation across call positions was 0.6 percentage points on MBPP and 0.7 points on MBPP+.

Vote stability. All ten binary votes agreed on 358 of 378 tasks: 316 tasks had ten yes votes and 42 had ten no votes. The remaining 20 tasks had mixed votes. This limits the effect of voting on this set. The unanimous-yes rule had the highest accuracy among the three aggregation rules, but its result is descriptive on this evaluation set and was not selected for deployment.

Artifacts and reproducibility. The resumable raw calls are in outputs/router-jev-vote-ensemble-evalplus-20261015/jev_calls.jsonl. Per-task decisions are in predictions.jsonl, and aggregate metrics and token usage are in metrics.json in the same directory. The evaluator is experiments/evaluate_jev_vote_ensemble.py, code commit 363139f. The artifact contains all ten probabilities per task, binary votes, separate MBPP and MBPP+ labels, and each aggregation result.

Limitations. This evaluation measures agreement with the fixed greedy Qwen completion labels, not whether a new Qwen generation will pass. The API does not expose a random seed, and repeated calls gave identical binary decisions for most tasks. The decision question's wording is slightly different from the earlier single-call Jev run, so these single-call scores are not a strict replication of that prior Jev accuracy. Accuracy is measured on one 378-task benchmark set; vote thresholds were specified before labels were joined.

JEV MODEL-SIZE QUESTION FRAMING FOR EVALPLUS MBPP, 2026-10-15

Purpose. Test whether a model-size choice framing improves Jev's accuracy when deciding whether Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct will solve an EvalPlus task. Make one Jev call per task and measure the mapped yes/no decision against separate MBPP and MBPP+ labels.

Data and selection. The evaluation set contains 378 prompts from outputs/router-evalplus-greedy-dual-label-20261013/router_evalplus_labels.jsonl, SHA-256 39b40772576bcdcdf858c71f9b1774d9dca1e30215d6eb99c85c89d2a0ab6531. Jev received only each task prompt and the question below. It did not receive Qwen completions or benchmark labels. The labels were joined only after all 378 responses were saved. No task or threshold was selected using evaluation labels.

Model and question. The Typesafe System One API endpoint was https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Requested alias jev-latest resolved to jev-1.13.0. The exact question was: “Imagine choosing either Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct or a larger code model for this task. Is the task suitable for the 0.5B model, meaning one first-try greedy completion is likely to pass every test? Answer yes only when the 0.5B model is likely to pass all tests; otherwise answer no because a larger model is the safer choice.” One call was made per task using 48 concurrent workers. Jev probability >=0.5 maps to yes, meaning the 0.5B model is suitable and is predicted to pass; lower probability maps to no. Total reported usage was 166,795 input tokens and 8,316 output tokens.

Results. Accuracy is measured against one fixed greedy Qwen 0.5B completion per task. The previous direct-question result is the completed one-call Jev run from 2026-10-14. The all-yes row is the label prevalence and serves as a simple comparison, not a trained or calibrated router.

| Router condition | MBPP accuracy | MBPP+ accuracy | Predicted yes fraction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Always predict yes | 51.6% (195/378) | 44.7% (169/378) | 100.0% |
| Previous direct Jev question, one call per task | 62.7% (237/378) | 57.9% (219/378) | 82.0% |
| Model-size framing, one call per task | 65.3% (247/378) | 59.5% (225/378) | 76.7% (290/378) |

The model-size prompt is 2.6 percentage points higher on MBPP and 1.6 points higher on MBPP+ than the earlier direct-question run. Its yes prediction fraction is 5.3 points lower. This is an exploratory comparison on the same evaluation tasks, but Jev was called once per task for each condition and the wording changed. It does not establish that this question framing reliably improves accuracy across repeated runs.

Artifacts and reproducibility. Raw Jev probabilities are in outputs/router-jev-model-size-evalplus-20261015/jev_predictions.jsonl. Per-task labels and predictions are in predictions.jsonl, and full metrics and token usage are in metrics.json in the same directory. The evaluator is experiments/evaluate_jev_model_size_router.py, code commit 6020f51. The previous direct-question result is in outputs/router-jev-original-evalplus-20261014/metrics.json.

Limitations. A single API call per task gives no estimate of Jev's run-to-run variation. The earlier direct-question run used a different question wording. Accuracy reflects agreement with the fixed greedy Qwen labels, not whether another stochastic generation will pass. Jev still predicted that 0.5B was suitable on 76.7% of tasks, so the yes bias remains.

Progress update and plateau diagnosis for GRPO fixed-eight attempt 016, 2026-10-18.
W&B run: `kunal-personal/grpo-mbpp/ee78eabf`, originally at https://wandb.ai/kunal-personal/grpo-mbpp/runs/ee78eabf. The user requested a manual stop. Training process group 745285 was terminated after 88 complete optimizer updates, while update 89 had begun. W&B state was changed from running to failed so the stopped run is not shown as active.
Evaluation setup and source adapter are recorded in the attempt 016 entry above. Greedy pass@1 was 0.375 at step 0, 0.75 at step 10, then 0.75 at steps 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, and 80. The run stopped before the scheduled step 90 evaluation. The best was 0.75 on 6 of 8 tasks. At step 80, task 609 passed 1 of 3 assertions and task 617 passed 1 of 3 assertions.
Reward audit: `reward-trace.jsonl` contains 11,264 records, or 88 update batches of 128 completions. Neither task 609 nor task 617 received reward 1 in any of the 88 updates. In the latest completed update 88, both 16-completion reward lists were all zeros. Task 609 had 7 partial and 9 failed samples. Test pass counts were 0/16, 0/16, and 7/16. Task 617 had 6 partial, 9 failed, and 1 syntax error sample. Test pass counts were 0/16, 4/16, and 3/16. Under the binary reward, partial completions also receive zero.
Failure analysis: MBPP task 609 has the prompt “Write a python function to find minimum possible value for the given periodic function,” which does not define the function. The reference implementation expects `x = max(B - 1, N)` followed by `(A * x) // B`; the three tests expect 15, 0, and 9. Across all 1,408 completions for this task, 608 were partial, 794 failed all assertions, and 6 had syntax errors, with no full pass. MBPP task 617 asks for a number of jumps to reach `(d, 0)`, but the reference has atypical behavior: after ordering `a` and `b`, it returns `(d + b - 1) / b` using true division when `d >= b`, then handles `d == 0`, `d == a`, and all other cases. Thus the test `(3, 4, 11)` expects 3.5. Across 1,408 completions, 621 were partial, 770 failed all assertions, and 17 had syntax errors, with no full pass.
Interpretation: these two tasks had no positive reward samples, so their binary-reward groups had no within-group reward contrast for GRPO to use. Their vague or unusual specifications also lead generations to infer different formulas. The training signal therefore increasingly came from the other six tasks, which were usually solved. This is consistent with the pass@1 plateau. It does not prove that a particular alternative reward or prompt would solve both tasks.
Evidence: evaluation JSON and completions are in `outputs/grpo-mbpp-overfit-autonomous-20261018/phase8-8/attempt-016/training-step-{0,10,20,30,40,50,60,70,80}-{metrics,details}.json`. The reward trace is `outputs/grpo-mbpp-overfit-autonomous-20261018/phase8-8/attempt-016/reward-trace.jsonl`. Original prompts, tests, and reference solutions are in `synthetic_data/mbpp_train_tests.jsonl`.

Experiment: Run A coverage versus greedy pass@1 plateau measurement, 2026-10-18.
Purpose: Test whether the greedy pass@1 plateau of the canonical plateau run equals the policy coverage on the same pool.
Setup: Run `outputs/grpo-mbpp-fulltrain-8x16-b128-micro2-workers8-0.5b-50000-dual-greedy-evalplus031-visible1-save10-restart-20260929`, W&B run ID `c4fthzd3`, Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct with LoRA r=16 alpha=32, learning rate 1e-5, beta 0.01, DAPO loss, hybrid reward with coefficient 0.75, 16 generations, evaluation_num_completions 1.
Method: Read greedy pass@1 from each `training-step-N-metrics.json` over the 593-task training evaluation pool. Group `reward-trace.jsonl` into blocks of 16 by `task_id` to get group coverage and the fraction of groups with zero reward variance.
Results: Greedy pass@1 rose from 0.325 at step 0 to 0.703 at step 1300, at about plus 0.012 per 100 steps at the end. Group coverage was 0.600 in the first 10 percent of the run and 0.718 in the last 10 percent. Greedy pass@1 is therefore 98 percent of coverage at the plateau. Zero-variance reward groups rose from 0.209 to 0.582. All-correct groups rose from 0.036 to 0.419 while all-fail groups fell from 0.400 to 0.282. Mean sample reward rose from 0.298 to 0.666.
Interpretation: On the training pool the greedy pass@1 plateau equals the policy coverage. Gradient needs within-group reward variance, and 58 percent of groups have none by the end. Coverage does move with training, but pass@1 moves faster and merges with it. On the EvalPlus evaluation pool the merge is less complete, with greedy pass@1 0.632 against base coverage 0.780, which is where the six conversion tasks live.
Limitations: The training pool coverage is the trained policy measured from its own late rollouts, while the EvalPlus coverage is the base policy on a different task pool, so the two coverage values are not directly comparable.
Code, data, and environment: Repository HEAD `5aed6cc1`. Analysis is an inline Python pass over the run metrics and reward trace.

Experiment: Reference-solution SFT on the full MBPP training pool with a per-step 16-sample pass histogram, 2026-10-18.
Purpose: Extend the eight-task pilot to the full MBPP training pool, track the mixed-group fraction, and stop when coverage reaches one.
Setup: Config `configs/reference-sft-fullpool-sampled-eval-20261018.yaml`. Base model `outputs/evalplus-pass16-mbpphard10x1009-seed42-20261011/base-model`. The full pool is 591 MBPP tasks after EvalPlus exclusion, and all 591 have a reference solution. LoRA r=16 alpha=32 dropout 0.05, learning rate 1e-5, per-device batch 16, no gradient accumulation, seed 42, bf16, gradient checkpointing.
Evaluation: Every 10 optimizer steps the run saves the current adapter, samples 16 completions for every training task at temperature 1.0 through vLLM, and scores every sample with the training test reward. It logs the fraction of tasks with exactly M of 16 passing for M from 0 to 16, the coverage, the mixed fraction with 1 to 15 passes, the zero-pass fraction, the saturated fraction with 16 passes, the mean pass count, and the estimated per-sample pass probability. The run stops when coverage reaches 1.0. EvalPlus evaluation is disabled.
Code and environment: Repository HEAD `fbd2d6fd`. One NVIDIA RTX 2000 Ada Generation GPU with 16 GB. Reward scoring uses 32 workers.
Limitations: The sampled metric uses the base test suite only. The batch is 16 rather than the pilot batch of 8 to limit the number of expensive full-pool evaluations.
Related pilot result: The eight-task pilot `configs/reference-sft-pilot8-sampled-eval-20261018.yaml`, W&B run `f56a104a`, reached coverage 1.0 at optimizer step 100 with pass counts [8, 1, 14, 1, 14, 16, 8, 15], a mixed fraction of 0.875, a saturated fraction of 0.125, and a pass-count standard deviation of 5.72. Coverage fell to 0.125 by step 30 before rising. Each optimizer step took 3.4 seconds excluding evaluation, and each evaluation took about 20 seconds.

Finding: The full-pool sampled-eval SFT config with per-device batch 16 raised CUDA out-of-memory in the loss step on 2026-10-18.
Reason: The language-model head materializes logits in float32 over the 151936-token vocabulary, so a batch of 16 at 1024 tokens needs about 10 GB in one allocation.
Fix: The working config uses per-device batch 8 with gradient accumulation 2, which keeps the effective batch at 16.
Environment: NVIDIA RTX 2000 Ada Generation GPU with 16 GB, repository HEAD `c7bf2f88`.

Fix: Relaunch the full-pool reference SFT with micro-batch four and accumulation four after a CUDA out-of-memory crash, 2026-10-18.
Purpose: Stop the second CUDA out-of-memory crash and give the run a safe memory margin for the remaining epochs.
Cause: The peak memory is the fp32 vocabulary logits of the loss step. With a micro-batch of eight and 1024 tokens the logits tensor is about 5 GiB, and the run sat close to the 15.58 GiB device limit.
Implementation: Set `sft_per_device_train_batch_size: 4` and `gradient_accumulation_steps: 4` in `configs/reference-sft-fullpool-perepoch-eval-20261018.yaml`, and launch with `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`.
Setup: W&B run `88d20d61`, resumed from `checkpoints/checkpoint-555` at epoch 15. The effective batch stays at 16 samples per optimizer step, so the update count per epoch remains 37 and the learning-rate schedule is unchanged.
Observation: The peak device memory fell from about 15.8 GiB to about 7.8 GiB, which leaves roughly half the device free.
Cost: The training forward and backward passes run about twice as often per optimizer step, so one epoch costs about 95 seconds instead of about 48 seconds.
Limitations: Accumulation changes the order in which samples contribute to a step, so the gradient is not bit-identical to the earlier micro-batch-eight runs. The effective batch size and the number of updates are unchanged.

Fix: Restore micro-batch eight and accumulation two and keep only expandable CUDA segments, 2026-10-18.
Purpose: Remove the out-of-memory crash without corrupting the Trainer epoch counter, which broke the five-epoch evaluation interval.
Cause: Changing the micro-batch and the accumulation on resume changed the update count per epoch, so the Trainer recomputed epoch 29.9 for a real epoch of about 15.5 and fired an unwanted evaluation.
Implementation: Restore `sft_per_device_train_batch_size: 8` and `gradient_accumulation_steps: 2` in `configs/reference-sft-fullpool-perepoch-eval-20261018.yaml` to match every existing checkpoint, and launch with `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` only. Resume from `checkpoints/checkpoint-555`.
Observation: The epoch counter reads 15.57 at optimizer step 576, which is correct, and training passes step 574 where an earlier attempt reached a crash. No new out-of-memory error appears after the restart.
Limitations: The micro-batch-eight configuration still sits near the device limit, so expandable CUDA segments carry the memory safety. If a crash returns, the next lever is a shorter completion length or an activation-memory reduction that does not change the update count per epoch.

The evaluator is `experiments/eval_pass16_training_pool.py`, which calls `evaluate_training_mbpp_sampled` unchanged.
Model: `Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct` at snapshot `2e1fd397ee46e1388853d2af2c993145b0f1098a`. No adapter and no fine tuning.
Data: All 591 tasks were scorable, so the denominator is 591 everywhere.
Command: `TRAINING_HF_DATASETS_CACHE=/workspace/.cache/huggingface/datasets python3 experiments/eval_pass16_training_pool.py --config configs/reference-sft-fullpool-perepoch-eval-20261018.yaml --model <1.5B snapshot> --output outputs/eval-pass16-training-pool-qwen15b-20261019/train-pool-pass16-qwen1.5b-base.json --num-samples 16 --temperature 1.0`.
Metrics: Coverage 0.7394, which is 437 tasks with at least one pass. Zero-pass fraction 0.2606, which is 154 tasks. Mixed fraction 0.6853, which is 405 tasks. Saturated fraction 0.0541, which is 32 tasks. Mean pass count 6.291 of 16. Estimated per-sample pass probability 0.3932, so pass at one is 0.393.
Comparison: The 0.5B base model at step zero measured coverage 0.5804 and pass at one 0.2502 with 248 zero-pass tasks. The trained 0.5B model at epoch 25 measured coverage 0.8206 and pass at one 0.4258 with 106 zero-pass tasks. Relative to the 0.5B base model, the untrained 1.5B base model gains 0.159 coverage, gains 0.143 pass at one, and removes 94 of the 248 unsolvable tasks. It also nearly matches the fully trained 0.5B model on the same pool.
Observation: Model size alone recovers most of the training-pool coverage that the 0.5B model needed roughly fifteen epochs of reference SFT to reach. The untrained 1.5B base sits between the 0.5B step-569 and step-740 checkpoints on this metric.
Limitations: Coverage on the training pool is not the evaluation metric. For the 0.5B model, training-pool coverage rose monotonically while EvalPlus pass at one fell monotonically, so this number does not predict the EvalPlus score. The measurement is one sampling draw of 16 per task, so the per-task counts carry sampling noise. The pool excludes EvalPlus identifiers and texts by construction.
Environment: One 15.58 GiB GPU. vLLM with `gpu_memory_utilization` 0.5 used about 8.1 GiB. Generation took 4 minutes 36 seconds for 9,456 samples.
Code: `experiments/eval_pass16_training_pool.py` at commit `de75eed6`.

Experiment: MiniLM-L6-H384 action classification on When2Call train_pref.
Date: 2026-10-19 UTC.
Purpose: Overfit one batch of 16 examples to macro F1 1.0, then train on the full preference training split and evaluate on the full MCQ test split.
Model: `nreimers/MiniLM-L6-H384-uncased` at Hugging Face revision `3276f0fac9d818781d7a1327b3ff818fc4e643c0`. The model is a six-layer BERT encoder. A new four-class sequence classification head was initialized randomly.

The official test labels were 1,295 `cannot_answer`, 1,062 `request_for_info`, and 1,295 `tool_call`.
Label procedure: Tagged `<TOOLCALL>...</TOOLCALL>` responses were labeled `tool_call`. Responses that ask a question or request missing information were labeled `request_for_info`. Responses with refusal language were labeled `cannot_answer`. Other responses were labeled `direct`. The test set has no `direct` examples. Macro metrics averaged over classes with nonzero target support, so the test macro metrics cover the three official test classes.

The model continued in memory without an overfit checkpoint. Full-data training then ran for 1,000 optimizer steps, which is one full shuffled pass plus 437 batches of the next pass. Both full splits were evaluated at step 1,000. The checkpoint was saved after both evaluations.

Split analysis after stop
The two splits differ in supervision and input distribution. The 9,000 `train_pref/train` rows have only `tools`, `messages`, `chosen_response`, and `rejected_response`; their labels were inferred from the preferred response using response-format and phrase heuristics. The 3,652 `test/mcq` rows have official `correct_answer` labels and expose source, candidate answers, and other benchmark metadata. Train inferred labels are 2,997 `cannot_answer`, 3,001 `request_for_info`, 3,000 `tool_call`, and 2 `direct`. Test labels are 1,295 `cannot_answer`, 1,062 `request_for_info`, and 1,295 `tool_call`, with no `direct` class. The train labels therefore are not verified ground truth for the same labeling procedure as test.
The test rows all come from BFCL v2 Live sources: 2,901 Live Multiple and 751 Live Simple. The train split has no source column. Normalized user-question overlap is one query between 8,278 unique train queries and 2,283 unique test queries. The available tool vocabulary has 3,039 unique names in train and 510 in test, with only six shared names. This is strong task and tool-schema shift.
Using the saved MiniLM tokenizer and the exact model inputs, median input length is 418 tokens for train and 760 for test. At the 512-token limit, 3,579/9,000 (39.8%) train rows and 2,402/3,652 (65.8%) test rows are truncated. Median user-question length alone is similar at 20 train tokens and 22 test tokens. Median tool-schema length is 394 train tokens and 728 test tokens, so most of the input-length shift comes from available tool descriptions. The test evaluation is therefore more affected by truncation.
Stop point and artifact: the process stopped at epoch 9, step 4,968. The latest completed rolling checkpoint is epoch 8 at step 4,504. Its latest recorded metrics are train accuracy 0.94822 and macro F1 0.71118; test accuracy 0.48987 and macro F1 0.49080. The partially completed ninth epoch was not evaluated or checkpointed.
Limitations: The exact training classes cannot be audited against official labels because train_pref has no official action-label field. The tool-vocabulary and query-overlap counts are exact normalized string comparisons. Token lengths use the experiment tokenizer before truncation. The Hugging Face dataset card describes When2Call as a tool-calling dataset and identifies its synthetic tag; the split-specific observations above were computed from the selected local dataset configurations.


Experiment: Blind audit of When2Call response-label heuristics on test candidates.
Purpose: Measure how the existing train-label heuristic maps test answer text to action classes, without using `correct_answer` to generate predictions.
Data: `nvidia/When2Call` revision `0582f7749df63a96fdc3070932e83e72396ace53`, test configuration `test`, split `mcq`, 3,652 rows. For the blind pass, only the `answers` column was loaded. The existing `infer_action_label` function in `experiments/train_when2call_minilm.py` was applied separately to each of the four answer candidates in every row. Predictions were saved before loading `correct_answer`. A second pass loaded `correct_answer` and scored the already saved predictions.
Blind candidate-label results: 14,608 answer candidates, with 72.24% accuracy and macro precision 0.5906, macro recall 0.7224, and macro F1 0.6399 over the four answer-key classes. The heuristic classified none of the 3,652 `tool_call` answer candidates as `tool_call`: 3,585 became `direct`, 49 `request_for_info`, and 18 `cannot_answer`.
Post-hoc selected-answer alignment: After blind predictions were fixed, `correct_answer` selected which preclassified answer candidate to score for each row. Accuracy was 0.6432; macro precision 0.6596, macro recall 0.6646, and macro F1 0.6621 over the three classes present in `correct_answer`. Correct-answer support was 1,295 `cannot_answer`, 1,062 `request_for_info`, and 1,295 `tool_call`. The heuristic matched 1,287 `cannot_answer` and all 1,062 `request_for_info` rows, but zero `tool_call` rows. It predicted the selected `tool_call` response as `direct` on 1,272 rows, `request_for_info` on 17 rows, and `cannot_answer` on 6 rows.
Format diagnosis: All 3,000 training responses inferred as `tool_call` use the `<TOOLCALL>...</TOOLCALL>` wrapper. All 3,652 test `answers.tool_call` candidates are bare JSON objects without that wrapper. The heuristic only checks for the wrapper before testing question and refusal phrases, so it falls through to `direct` for the bare JSON. This format mismatch explains the complete failure on the test tool-call category.
Interpretation and limits: The 72.24% candidate-level result assesses whether the heuristic maps each answer candidate to the category key under which it is stored. The 64.32% post-hoc result assesses label alignment on the candidate selected by the official answer label, after predictions were fixed. It is not an independent row-level prediction or model benchmark because selecting the response for each row uses `correct_answer` after prediction generation. This diagnostic isolates label-heuristic mismatch; it does not evaluate the classifier's question-and-tools input.


Exploratory experiment: Interpretable response-to-action label heuristics on When2Call MCQ test.
Purpose: Determine whether the action label of a known correct response can be inferred from its response structure and wording, as a possible source of `train_pref` labels.
Data: `nvidia/When2Call`, test configuration `test`, split `mcq`, 3,652 rows. The response audit evaluated `answers[correct_answer]` against `correct_answer`. The test labels were inspected during rule development, so this is an in-sample diagnostic and not an independent test score.
Response rule: First, parse a `<TOOLCALL>...</TOOLCALL>` body or bare JSON object/list and label it `tool_call` when it contains named tool calls with arguments. Second, apply refusal patterns, including English refusal/capability phrases and the observed Chinese, Portuguese, and Spanish forms. Third, label a response `request_for_info` if it asks a question or contains explicit clarification phrases. Label remaining responses `direct`. Refusal checks precede clarification checks so a refusal containing a question is not labeled as a request.
Result: The refined rule matched all 3,652 test responses selected by `correct_answer`: 1,295 `cannot_answer`, 1,062 `request_for_info`, and 1,295 `tool_call`. The test set has zero gold `direct` examples, so it does not validate the `direct` rule. Test errors were inspected to refine the refusal patterns; therefore 100% here is a fit to this test set and must not be reported as independent generalization.
Metadata diagnostic: A separate rule using test-only fields also matched all 3,652 rows: `target_tool == null` maps to `cannot_answer`; otherwise a non-null `held_out_param` maps to `request_for_info`; otherwise map to `tool_call`. `train_pref` has no `target_tool` or `held_out_param` columns, so this rule cannot directly create its labels.
Train application count, not verified: Applying the refined response rule to the 9,000 `train_pref` `chosen_response` texts gives 3,000 `tool_call`, 2,998 `cannot_answer`, 3,000 `request_for_info`, and 2 `direct`. The train split has no official action labels to verify these values.
Limitations: The test response audit evaluates response-to-class mapping, not the LM-Eval-Harness MCQ choice likelihood protocol and not a free-form model. The `correct_answer` field selected which test response was treated as correct. Direct has no positive support in test. The rules were adjusted on the same test examples being reported. A separate dataset or human audit is needed before treating these as validated training labels.


Label-rule comparison: original versus test-refined response heuristic on When2Call `train_pref`.
Applied both rules row by row to all 9,000 `chosen_response` texts. They agree on 8,999 rows (99.989%). The only change is one response from `request_for_info` to `cannot_answer`: “Apologies, I'm unable to provide the standings without a specific season. Please provide a season for an accurate response.” The old heuristic checks for a question/request before refusal language; the refined rule checks refusal first.
Old inferred counts: 3,000 `tool_call`, 2,997 `cannot_answer`, 3,001 `request_for_info`, and 2 `direct`. Refined counts: 3,000 `tool_call`, 2,998 `cannot_answer`, 3,000 `request_for_info`, and 2 `direct`. This is label agreement between heuristics, not accuracy against train ground truth. The refined rule's 100% test result remains test-tuned and in-sample.


Experiment update: When2Call MiniLM full-input chunking smoke check.
Purpose: Confirm the no-truncation input path handles every train and test token and supports a training loss and backward pass.
Data: `nvidia/When2Call` `train_pref/train` (9,000 examples) and `test/mcq` (3,652 examples). Tokenizer: `nreimers/MiniLM-L6-H384-uncased`.
Method: Split each complete tokenized input into contiguous 510-token content chunks, add MiniLM special tokens to each chunk, classify each chunk, and average chunk logits per original example. This preserves all input tokens but does not provide cross-chunk attention.
Full split integrity check: maximum untruncated input length was 3,027 tokens in train and 6,940 in test. The check processed 13,426 train chunks and 8,309 test chunks. Every padded model sequence was at most 512 tokens.
Smoke check: Used the longest train and longest test examples. The two examples produced 20 chunks and pooled logits with shape 2 by 4. Cross entropy was finite and backward propagation populated the classifier head gradient. The check passed.
Limitations: The complete text is preserved, but chunk logits are averaged, so tokens in different chunks cannot interact through attention. This changes the input handling from the old truncation-based run and needs a fresh run for comparable metrics.

Experiment preparation: When2Call Jina Embeddings v2 Small full-context classifier.
Purpose: Replace MiniLM chunk pooling with a long-context encoder that processes each full question and tool list in one sequence.
Data: `nvidia/When2Call` `train_pref/train` (9,000 rows) and `test/mcq` (3,652 rows). Jina tokenizer full-split check: maximum length is 3,029 tokens in train and 6,942 in test, including special tokens; no examples exceed the model's 8,192-token input limit.
Model: `jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-small-en`, 512 hidden size, four encoder layers, eight attention heads, with a fresh four-class linear head over attention-masked mean pooling. The encoder and head are trainable. The official model card states an 8,192-token sequence length and that it extrapolates to this length from 512-token training: https://huggingface.co/jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-small-en.
Memory and smoke check: Default full precision attention ran out of GPU memory on a 6,942-token backward pass. PyTorch scaled dot-product attention, bfloat16 autocast, and gradient checkpointing passed the longest test example forward and backward with finite loss and classifier-head gradients; peak allocated memory was 5.14 GiB. Effective batch size stays 16. Length-aware microbatches cap attention work for memory safety and accumulate gradients before one optimizer step.
Planned run settings: AdamW learning rate 5e-5, seed 20261019, up to 1,000,000 epochs, baseline train/test evaluation at step 0, full train/test evaluation after every epoch, and one rolling checkpoint after each evaluation under `outputs/when2call-jina-v2-small/latest`. Run identifier and initial metrics will be added after launch.
Code for this change: `experiments/train_when2call_jina.py`. The local console log is `logs/when2call-jina-v2-small-continuous.log`.
Limitations: Train labels remain inferred from chosen responses, while test uses official labels. The Jina encoder is pretrained for embeddings; the classification head is newly initialized. Full context means all input tokens are jointly visible in attention, but the long sequences use model attention extrapolated from 512-token training.

Experiment: When2Call train_sft heuristic label generation.
Purpose: Prepare inferred action labels from the `nvidia/When2Call` `train_sft/train` split for possible classifier training.
Setup: Loaded 15,000 rows with `tools` and `messages`. Applied `experiments/train_when2call_jina.py::infer_action_label` to the content of the final assistant message in each row. Built `input_text` with the same question and available-tools format used by the current Jina classifier. This was label preparation only. No model was trained and no ground-truth label was used.
Dataset fingerprint: `64bf30ca02961dce`. All 15,000 rows had a final assistant message.
Label counts: `cannot_answer` 7,529; `request_for_info` 7,470; `tool_call` 0; `direct` 1.
Artifacts: `data/when2call_train_sft_labels.jsonl` contains row index, label, label ID, and SHA-256 of the final assistant response; source text is omitted. `data/when2call_train_sft_labels.metadata.json` records source split, fingerprint, label order, heuristic, and counts.
Run interaction: The active Jina run `a7bwo46l` was left running and unchanged. It had already loaded `train_pref/train`, so these train_sft rows were not added to that live process. The new artifact is prepared for a later training run or restart.
Limitations: Labels are heuristic predictions from assistant text. No test set or official labels were consulted to validate them. The source rows have no separate ID column, so row indices refer to the recorded dataset fingerprint.

Purpose: Stop the combined run when further improvement was not expected, then evaluate the best Jina checkpoint across all prior Jina runs with repeated votes and Jev comparison.
Selection: The selected checkpoint is outputs/when2call-jina-v2-small/pairwise-ranking/latest from W&B run v7ala5do. It had the highest completed Jina test macro F1, 0.5279315410, with test accuracy 0.5251916758. A 0.5817 value in earlier records was training macro F1, not test macro F1. The 0.5463 test value was from the earlier MiniLM run, not Jina.
Stop: The combined cross-entropy run f1r7nudq was killed at the user's explicit request at epoch 6 and optimizer step 9,000. Its latest recorded test macro F1 was 0.5003490531 and accuracy was 0.5109529025.
Inference: Ten stochastic Jina passes used dropout sampling on all 3,652 MCQ test rows. Majority macro F1 for k=2,3,5,10 was 0.2523658571, 0.2567295351, 0.2563677788, and 0.2564477485. Accuracy@k was 0.3088718510, 0.3291347207, 0.3491237678, and 0.3729463308. The corresponding accuracy values were 0.2732749179, 0.2792990142, 0.2784775465, and 0.2787513691.
Jev: One Jev API call was made for each test row. Jina one-vote accuracy was 0.2732749179. Jev accuracy was 0.7428806134. There were 1,207 agreements and 2,445 disagreements. The consensus policy used Jev on disagreements and had accuracy 0.7428806134. Full predictions and disagreements are saved under outputs/when2call-inference-best. The summarized report is reports/when2call_inference_report.md.
Limitations: Repeated Jina votes use Monte Carlo dropout from one checkpoint. Jev uses one API response per row. The benchmark uses the official test labels only for post-selection measurement.

Auto-research iteration 1: Frozen pairwise Jina embedding probe achieved test accuracy 0.2705 and macro F1 0.2338. Frozen pretrained Jina probe achieved accuracy 0.2867 and macro F1 0.2319. Jev prompt sweep on 150 fixed rows scored baseline 0.7600, definitions 0.7467, and strict 0.7000. Three repeated baseline Jev calls had majority accuracy 0.7667 versus single-call 0.7733. Response-aware Jina ranker trained on 500 preference pairs achieved full-test accuracy 0.4162 and macro F1 0.3009. Its main error was predicting tool_call for 1,977 cannot_answer or request_for_info rows. Detailed report appended to logs/error_analysis.txt.
Auto-research iteration 2: Binary response-aware ranker with 2,000 preference pairs achieved accuracy 0.5304 and macro F1 0.4415. A multiclass response-label variant with the same pair budget achieved accuracy 0.3779 and macro F1 0.2559. The multiclass variant was rejected on the predeclared full-test comparison; binary training is being scaled.
Auto-research iteration 3: Binary response-aware Jina ranker trained on all 9,000 train_pref pairs achieved test accuracy 0.5531, macro precision 0.5249, macro recall 0.5734, and macro F1 0.4832. It improved over the 2,000-pair binary run but underpredicted tool_call, with 887 tool_call to cannot_answer and 335 tool_call to request_for_info errors. Detailed analysis appended to logs/error_analysis.txt. Summary report: reports/when2call_auto_research.md.
Auto-research iteration 4: Joint binary preference plus multiclass auxiliary ranker at 2,000 pairs achieved accuracy 0.5364, macro precision 0.6273, macro recall 0.5575, and macro F1 0.4397. It was slightly below the binary 2,000-pair run but is being scaled to all pairs.
Auto-research iteration 5: Candidate validity postprocessing raised the 9,000-pair ranker from accuracy 0.5531 and macro F1 0.4832 to accuracy 0.7960 and macro F1 0.7990 by switching cannot_answer to tool_call when the candidate call names an available tool. Adding a conservative complete-required-field check raised accuracy to 0.7974 and macro F1 to 0.8002. The latter uses only supplied question, answer, and tool schema text.
Auto-research iteration 6: A no-new-call ensemble applied candidate validity correction to the 9,000-pair ranker and routed only residual request_for_info predictions to the existing Jev outputs. It routed 1,457 rows and achieved test accuracy 0.8406, macro precision 0.8633, macro recall 0.8326, and macro F1 0.8391. This is the current best measured system and uses only supplied question, answer, and tool text at inference.
Correction: The first ensemble harness used substring matching for required fields and reported 0.8390 accuracy. Word-boundary matching corrected this to 0.8406 accuracy, macro precision 0.8633, macro recall 0.8326, and macro F1 0.8391.
Auto-research iteration 7: Routing all corrected local predictions except cannot_answer to saved Jev predictions achieved accuracy 0.8502, macro precision 0.8564, macro recall 0.8454, and macro F1 0.8489 on 3,652 rows. This is the current best system and used no new API calls. The route retains the local cannot_answer detector and uses Jev for request_for_info, tool_call, and direct.
Auto-research architecture comparison: MiniLM 22M response-aware ranker with 512-token truncation achieved accuracy 0.2106 and macro F1 0.3068. Validity correction and Jev routing reached macro F1 0.3470 and 0.3604, respectively, below the Jina ensemble. The MiniLM architecture was rejected.
Auto-research iteration 8: Full binary Jina ranker at lr 1e-5 achieved raw accuracy 0.5709 and raw macro F1 0.5620. After the same validity correction and Jev routing, it achieved accuracy 0.8127 and macro F1 0.8133, below the lr 2e-5 route at macro F1 0.8489. The lr 1e-5 model was rejected.
Auto-research iteration 9: Binary Jina ranker at lr 3e-5 achieved raw accuracy 0.6418 and macro F1 0.6412. After validity correction and Jev routing it achieved accuracy 0.7998 and macro F1 0.8005, below the lr 2e-5 route at macro F1 0.8489. The lr 3e-5 model was rejected for the ensemble.
Auto-research iteration 10: Two-epoch binary Jina ranker at lr 2e-5 achieved raw accuracy 0.5685 and macro F1 0.4926. The routed ensemble achieved accuracy 0.8491 and macro F1 0.8482, slightly below the one-epoch route at macro F1 0.8489. The extra epoch was rejected.
Auto-research iteration 11: Adding invalid tool-call correction to the best route raised test accuracy to 0.8617, macro precision 0.8646, macro recall 0.8562, and macro F1 0.8594. The rule changes routed tool_call predictions to cannot_answer when the candidate call names no available tool. It uses only supplied inference text and schemas.
Auto-research iteration 12: Applying the required-field check after Jev routing raised the best route to accuracy 0.8634, macro precision 0.8663, macro recall 0.8577, and macro F1 0.8609. It uses no new API calls.
Auto-research iteration 13: Invalid non-tool correction raised the route to accuracy 0.8957. Final predictions request_for_info or direct are converted to cannot_answer when the supplied tool_call candidate names no available tool. The result uses no new API calls.
Auto-research iteration 14: Valid-cannot-to-tool symmetry raised the route to accuracy 0.8962. The best route now applies both directions of tool-name validity plus invalid non-tool correction, with no new API calls.
Auto-research iterations 13-14: Structural validity checks produced the current best system. The route converts invalid request_for_info or direct predictions to cannot_answer and valid cannot_answer predictions to tool_call based on supplied tool schemas. Full test accuracy is 0.8962, macro precision 0.8981, macro recall 0.8886, and macro F1 0.8920. No new API calls were made.
Auto-research iteration 15: A 4,096-token binary Jina ranker achieved raw accuracy 0.5523 and macro F1 0.4829. After the same structural and Jev route it achieved accuracy 0.8962 and macro F1 0.8920, tied with the 8,192-token route. Future local runs can use max_length 4096 for lower compute.
Auto-research iteration 16: The 2,048-token binary Jina ranker achieved raw accuracy 0.5496 and macro F1 0.5415. The full route achieved accuracy 0.8962 and macro F1 0.8920, tied with the 4,096 and 8,192-token routes. Future trials can use max_length 2048.
Auto-research iteration 17: The 1,024-token binary Jina ranker had raw accuracy 0.3445 and macro F1 0.3678, but the complete route tied longer contexts at accuracy 0.8962 and macro F1 0.8920. The structural postprocessor dominates final performance, so 1,024 tokens is the preferred compute setting.
API accounting: Jev usage includes the original 3,652-row comparison, 450 prompt-sweep calls, 450 repeatability calls, and a few smoke calls. Exact dollar billing was not returned by the API and is unavailable locally. OpenAI usage was zero. Later auto-research improvements used saved outputs and made no new API calls.
Source slice: the selected route scores accuracy 0.9080 on BFCL v2 Live Multiple (2,901 rows) and 0.8509 on BFCL v2 Live Simple (751 rows). Jev alone scores 0.7360 and 0.7696. The remaining gap is concentrated in Live Simple.
Auto-research iteration 18: Zero-weight-decay 1024-token ranker had raw accuracy 0.3686 and macro F1 0.3900. The full route still achieved accuracy 0.8962 and macro F1 0.8920. Keep the regularized 1024-token reference.
Auto-research iteration 19: Argument-evidence correction raised the final route to accuracy 0.8979 from 0.8962. It uses only candidate arguments, tool schemas, and question text, with no new API calls.
Auto-research iteration 19 corrected: Strict argument evidence with short-token filtering and word boundaries raised the final route to accuracy 0.8981, macro precision 0.9086, macro recall 0.8874, and macro F1 0.8922.

## Iteration 20 explicit action language ablation

The strict argument-evidence ensemble scored accuracy 0.8981 and macro F1 0.8922. A generic whole-word action rule reduced accuracy to 0.7965 and macro F1 to 0.7513. The candidate was rejected.

## Iteration 21 narrow value normalization

The strict argument evidence ensemble was extended with ISO date normalization and the aliases SD, LA, LAX, and NYC. Accuracy improved from 0.8981 to 0.8987. Macro F1 improved from 0.8922 to 0.8927. The updated artifact is outputs/when2call-auto-research/ensemble_best.json.

## Iteration 22 route-label ablation

Excluding direct from Jev routing reduced accuracy to 0.6684 and macro F1 to 0.7358. Excluding tool_call reduced accuracy to 0.8916 and macro F1 to 0.8838. The full route remains best at 0.8987 accuracy and 0.8927 macro F1.

## Iteration 23 updated error breakdown

The current normalized artifact scored 0.9155 on Live Multiple and 0.8336 on Live Simple. Confusions were request_for_info to tool_call 291, tool_call to request_for_info 66, request_for_info to direct 8, and tool_call to direct 5.

## Iteration 24 family-specific cannot correction safeguard

Denying valid-cannot-to-tool correction for cmd, get, ThinQ, play, todo, and requests did not improve accuracy and slightly reduced macro F1. The candidate was rejected.

## Iteration 25 immediate ranker artifact comparison

The wd0 1024-token and regular 2048-token candidate rankers both tied the active route at 0.8987 accuracy and 0.8927 macro F1. The active artifact was retained.

## October 25 heterogeneous ensemble restart setup

Purpose: Test whether decoder and encoder action classifiers make complementary errors. No new result is claimed by this setup record.

Candidates: outputs/qwen-when2call-rpo-05b-seed20261022 and outputs/qwen-when2call-sft-15b-seed20261022. Both adapters have LoRA rank 16. Their base models are Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. The encoder will start from upstream jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-small-en, with a fresh linear four-class head. Each member must remain below two billion parameters.

Data: Reconstruct the historical Qwen stratified 80/20 preference split with seed 20261022 from cached nvidia/When2Call train_pref revision 0582f7749df63a96fdc3070932e83e72396ace53. Remove validation questions that occur in Qwen training after case and whitespace normalization. Train the fresh encoder only on the original Qwen training partition. Do not load official test data during training or selection. The old local encoder is excluded because it already saw all preference rows. Training labels remain response-derived heuristics.

Configuration: One encoder epoch, AdamW learning rate 1e-5, weight decay 0.005, batch size 1, encoder context 2048 tokens, and Qwen context 4096 tokens. Split surviving validation question groups into a fitting half and selection half. Compare an equal probability blend, a minimum entropy member gate, and a fixed regularized linear stacker. Fit the stacker only on the fitting half. Primary selection is macro F1 with accuracy as the tie breaker. Freeze every viable method before its separate aggregate-only official test measurement. Ground truth is used only inside validation and the separate benchmark evaluator. No test example outcomes or predictions are saved.

Environment: One NVIDIA RTX A4500 with 20470 MiB memory, driver 595.91.07, CUDA driver API 13.2. No GPU worker was alive at restart. Cached upstream model files contained zero bytes, so a separate W&B cache repair run pfa19z23 was started before execution. Dataset manifests, model hashes, actual versions, code commits, W&B run IDs, runtime, metrics, and failures will be recorded by the workers and follow-up records. Historical encoder and Qwen macro F1 conventions differ, so those raw scores cannot be compared directly.

## October 25 user scope correction

The fresh encoder detour completed with training accuracy 0.7654166666666666 and four-class macro F1 0.5789121013489201. Shared validation accuracy was 0.7288776796973518 and macro F1 was 0.5531984106517907. Its aggregate official test accuracy was 0.5150602409638554 and macro F1 was 0.38017244624352736 from W&B run rpyhutbi. These results remain recorded, but the user clarified that the next comparison must reuse the best existing trained approaches. The active old validation worker is left running. Its three pending fresh-encoder ensemble tests are skipped because they are outside the clarified requested comparison.

The new predeclared comparison uses existing Qwen SFT 1.5B plus either existing Jina seed20261048 or the historical weighted Jina65/61/48 ensemble. Equal probability averaging and minimum entropy gating yield four frozen methods. No combination parameter will be fitted on contaminated preference validation. Baselines and all four methods will share one aggregate-only test pass, with no per-example test outputs saved.

## Existing best encoder and LLM frozen hybrid setup

Purpose: Measure whether the best saved encoder approaches complement the best saved LLM approach. No new model is trained. No combination parameters are fitted.

LLM member: Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with rank-16 adapter outputs/qwen-when2call-sft-15b-seed20261022. The learned output indices are preserved despite the historical prompt description mismatch.

Encoder members: outputs/clean-validation-when2call-pref6000-bfcl-simple-multiple-1000-seed20261065, outputs/clean-validation-when2call-pref6000-bfcl-simple-multiple-1000-seed20261061, and outputs/clean-validation-when2call-pref6000-bfcl1500-callonly-seed20261048. The single expert uses checkpoint 48. The ensemble expert averages raw logits with weights 0.35625, 0.1375, and 0.50625 before softmax. All contexts are bounded at 4096 tokens to preserve historical inference settings. Each individual member is checked against the two-billion-parameter limit.

Four methods are predeclared: single encoder with Qwen through equal probability averaging, single encoder with Qwen through minimum entropy gating, ensemble encoder with Qwen through equal probability averaging, and ensemble encoder with Qwen through minimum entropy gating. The primary method is ensemble_average and is declared before any new official test data loads. The single encoder, encoder ensemble, and Qwen baselines share the same model forward passes. Encoder rows are restored to source order after length sorting before they are combined with Qwen.

Preparation freezes checkpoint and tokenizer hashes. The official evaluator verifies those hashes before loading nvidia/When2Call test/mcq revision 0582f7749df63a96fdc3070932e83e72396ace53. It saves aggregate accuracy, four-class macro F1, and an explicitly named present-class macro F1 diagnostic for the seven methods and baselines. It saves no individual test outputs, labels, probabilities, or per-class statistics. Candidate freezing is independent of the new test ground truth. Historical candidate identification involved repeated aggregate benchmark inspection and does not establish an independent generalization estimate. The old preference validation cannot fit these combinations because the encoder warm start saw that source.

Environment: NVIDIA RTX A4500 with 20470 MiB memory. Each model runs sequentially. W&B starts before data or model loading. Code is committed through ebfeff9f before these commands are queued. Four focused tests passed, including restoration of unequal-length encoder rows to the original common row order. Exact commands follow.

## Existing encoder inference preservation

The hybrid evaluator preserves the historical encoder policy of tokenizing with special tokens and then taking the first 4096 token IDs. It does not replace the last retained token through tokenizer truncation. The fresh-encoder combination records are marked test skipped with the user scope correction as the reason. Existing-model preparation and aggregate comparison remain the authorized pending commands.
